tasks.task: Search for the differences between "fewer" and "less" in grammar section, and provide examples illustrating their correct usage from the Cambridge Dictionary.
tasks.answer: Per the Cambridge Dictionary grammar article "Less or fewer?" (https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/less-or-fewer): Difference: less and fewer are comparative quantifiers. Less is the comparative form of little and is used with uncountable nouns; fewer is the comparative form of few and is used with plural (countable) nouns. Before articles/demonstratives/possessives/pronouns, use "less of" with singular nouns and "fewer of" with plural nouns. Using less with plural countable nouns (e.g. "less pizzas") is common in informal speech but traditionally not considered correct. Examples from the article - less: "I do less work at weekends than I used to."; "It was funny to begin with, but as time went on, it became less of a joke." fewer: "Better cycle routes would mean fewer cars and fewer accidents."; "Fewer of them will be getting that information from newspapers which arrive hours after the news has occurred."; "Every year in Britain about 5,000 people die on the roads. Fewer are killed at work."

tasks.task: Use the Cambridge Dictionary to understand the rules for forming and using comparative and superlative adjectives in English Grammar, including example sentences.

Navigated from the homepage to the Grammar area, then to the article 'Comparison: adjectives (bigger, biggest, more interesting)' at https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/comparison-adjectives-bigger-biggest-more-interesting. Key rules extracted: (1) Comparative adjectives compare one person/thing with another ('than' is used); (2) Superlative adjectives describe one person/thing as having more of a quality than all others; (3) One-syllable adjectives take -er (comparative) and -est (superlative) suffixes; (4) 'the' is normally used before a superlative adjective; (5) Two-syllable adjectives ending in -y change y to i and take -ier/-iest; (6) Adjectives with three or more syllables use more/less (comparative) and most/least (superlative); (7) Some one-syllable adjectives are irregular (good/better/best, bad/worse/worst, far/farther-further/farthest-furthest); (8) Never combine more/most with -er/-est endings. Example sentences from the page: 'Josh is taller than his sister.', 'It's colder today than yesterday.', 'Sasha is older than Mark.', 'We were busier last week than this week.', 'The second lecture was more interesting than the first.', 'I'm more interested in music than sport.', 'The 'Silver Arrow' will be the fastest train in the world when it is built.', 'I think that's the biggest apple I've ever seen!', 'The most frightening film I've ever seen was Alfred Hitchcock's 'Psycho'.' tasks.task: Search for guidelines on using indirect speech in English, with examples of how to change direct speech to indirect speech, on the Cambridge Dictionary.
tasks.answer: Found the Cambridge Dictionary grammar guidelines on indirect speech at https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/reported-speech-indirect-speech ('Reported speech: indirect speech', English Grammar Today). Guidelines: indirect speech reports the content of what someone said rather than their exact words; reporting statements uses a that-clause (that often omitted informally), yes-no/alternative questions use if/whether-clauses in statement word order, wh-questions use a wh-clause without a question mark, and commands use a to-infinitive clause. Direct-to-indirect examples shown on the page: 'I'm tired,' I said. -> I told them (that) I was tired.; 'Are you ready?' the nurse asked Joel. -> The nurse asked Joel if/whether he was ready.; 'Leave at once!' they ordered. -> They ordered us to leave at once.

tasks.task: Use Cambridge Dictionary to understand the use of articles ('a', 'an', 'the') in English Grammar, including examples of usage with both countable and uncountable nouns.
tasks.answer: Used Cambridge Dictionary to understand English articles. On https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/a-an-and-the ('A/an and the' under Grammar > Nouns, pronouns and determiners > Determiners): 'a/an' is the indefinite article and 'the' is the definite article. 'A' is used before words beginning with a consonant sound (e.g., 'a car', 'a university') and 'an' before a vowel sound (e.g., 'an apple', 'an hour'). With countable nouns, articles are used with singular forms (e.g., 'I have a sister and a brother.', 'The lion roared.'); 'the' can also be used with plurals when specific. With uncountable nouns, 'a/an' is not used (e.g., 'The rice we bought in the Thai shop is much better than the one we bought in the supermarket.'); uncountable nouns take no article when general and 'the' when specific.
